subject: biology
title: Animal Physiology (HL) Adventure 1: Muscles and movement
welcome_lead: Today you'll slide actin and myosin filaments — and bend a joint.
meta_desc: Biology HL — striated muscle, sliding filament theory, ATP, sarcomere, antagonistic pairs.
final_note: You learned skeletal muscle contracts by myosin walking along actin (sliding filament theory), powered by ATP, with sarcomere shortening, and bones move by antagonistic pairs.

concepts.def: Z-line to Z-line unit of muscle
Blocks binding until Ca²⁺ moves it

walkthroughs.body_html:
Sarcomere = Z-line to Z-line.

- Thin filaments (actin + tropomyosin + troponin) — anchored at Z.
- Thick filaments (myosin) — in the middle (A band).
- I band — actin only.
- H zone — myosin only.

On contraction, H zone and I band shorten; A band stays the same.

1. Nerve signal → Ca²⁺ released from sarcoplasmic reticulum.
2. Ca²⁺ binds troponin → tropomyosin moves → actin binding sites exposed.
3. Myosin head (ADP-bound) binds actin → cross-bridge.
4. Power stroke pulls actin; ADP released.
5. ATP binds myosin → head detaches; ATP hydrolysed → head re-cocks.

Cycle continues until Ca²⁺ pumped back.

Synovial joint (e.g. elbow): cartilage cushions ends; synovial fluid lubricates.

Bones act as levers; muscles work in antagonistic pairs:

- Biceps (flexor) bends elbow.
- Triceps (extensor) straightens it.

Tendons attach muscle to bone; ligaments attach bone to bone.

mcqs.q: Which ion triggers exposure of actin binding sites?
During contraction, which sarcomere zone stays the same length?
Why is ATP described as an 'energy currency' rather than energy storage?
options: ATP is constantly made and broken down — it transfers energy between reactions rather than storing large amounts for later.
ATP is permanent and accumulates with age in cells.
Only Na+ moves during an action potential; K+ stays still.
Cells store large amounts of ATP for emergency use.

mcqs.q: During an action potential, do Na+ and K+ move through the same channels?
options: Na+ and K+ swap places through the same channel at the same time.
Larger animals always eat the next ones up, and there aren't enough giant animals.
Only Na+ moves during an action potential; K+ stays still.
No — voltage-gated Na+ channels open first (depolarisation, Na+ in), then voltage-gated K+ channels open (repolarisation, K+ out).

mcqs.q: Why are food chains usually limited to about 4 or 5 trophic levels?
options: There aren't enough types of animals to fill more trophic levels.
Only Na+ moves during an action potential; K+ stays still.
Larger animals always eat the next ones up, and there aren't enough giant animals.
Only ~10 percent of energy is transferred between trophic levels; eventually too little energy remains to support another level.

sequence.def: Impulse reaches the junction, depolarising the fibre
Ca2+ floods out of the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Ca2+ moves tropomyosin off actin's binding sites
Myosin heads attach to actin filaments
Myosin pulls actin inward; sarcomere shortens
ATP binds myosin, breaking the cross-bridge
